item.title: How Finite Brains Generalize Without Bound: Spatial Memory as a Universal Computer
item.description:
Relevance: 33% | Source: arXiv AI
Yuhang He, Si Wu
arXiv:2611.07920v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A child who learned to add small numbers adds numbers of any length. LSTMs and Transformers trained on short sequences fail on longer ones. We trace this to what learners read when deciding. A position, count or time takes new values as input grows: it is a coordinate, and a learner that reads one meets in every long input values its experience never covered. Whether two things are the same has the same two answers at every size: it is a coincidence, and a learner that reads only coincidences finds in a long input nothing that short inputs lacked, so finite experience fixes its rule for every size. The memory carries the size of the input and the rule stays finite, and this determines the memory a generalizing brain can have: a memory that grows while what the learner reads of it stays finite has to look the same from every place, so it is made of cycles, and the past is reached by asking what happened when the cycles last stood where they stand now. The cycles are the grid modules, the cells that detect their return the place cells, the records the hippocampal index; a prefrontal controller moves the cycles and never sees them. Reading only coincidences costs no power: what finite experience fixes in such a learner is what Turing machines compute in step with their input, which is why a circuit that evolved to find the way home can learn arithmetic and grammar. In a network of neurons this machine of cycles is the dynamics seen through its symmetry, and symbols are its invariants. Trained on strings up to 40 symbols, the machine solves five benchmark tasks that no LSTM or Transformer solves, among them duplication and binary addition, and beyond the reach of its cycles it fails on the curve the theory predicts. Given larger cycles after training, a machine that saw no string longer than five symbols reverses a string of a million without error. Its controllers run unchanged on neurons.

item.title: Memorable Decision Cues are More Associable With Value
item.description:
Relevance: 33% | Source: SocArXiv
Daphna Shohamy et al.
When making decisions, we must use the sensory cues available at the moment of choice to predict the values of our options. Yet little is known about how properties of these cues affect the choice process, particularly our ability to retrieve decision-relevant memories. Here, we test whether and how image memorability, the population likelihood of recognizing a particular image, influences memory-guided decisions. Across five pre-registered experiments, memorable cue images were not chosen more overall; instead, they predicted more accurate retrieval of associated values and more value-sensitive choices. We account for this pattern of behavior with a formal exemplar model in which distinctive cues suffer less interference from competing memories during retrieval of associated values. The model predicts, and our data confirm, two interactions: choices are more sensitive to value differences between memorable options, and a difference in memorability biases choices toward the more memorable option when both are high in value, but away from it when both are low. Finally, we find that the same pattern held for choices between common foods, suggesting that shared associative memory processes are recruited for choices involving both novel and highly familiar options. Together, our results suggest that more memorable cues are more associable with value, and provide a process-level account for how memorability influences downstream decisions.

item.title: Slow but not fast theta tACS modulation of hippocampal-cortical connectivity compresses temporal distance judgments
item.description:
Relevance: 33% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Wang, Y., Jing, Y., Ivacs, L., Duecker, F., De Weerd, P., van de Ven, V.
The temporal organization of episodic memory is thought to depend critically on the hippocampus, potentially coordinated by theta-band oscillations. Here, we used concurrent transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to examine whether slow theta stimulation (3 Hz) applied over the left parietal cortex modulates hippocampal-cortical functional connectivity during memory encoding, and how this relates to subsequent temporal memory performance. Twenty-seven participants encoded sequences of object-scene pairs that were presented either within a single context or across a context boundary, under different tACS conditions (3 Hz, 8 Hz, and no stimulation), and afterwards judged the temporal distance between item pairs. Behaviorally, 3 Hz stimulation led to significantly compressed temporal distance judgments compared to 8 Hz, suggesting altered temporal memory reconstruction. Further, 3 Hz tACS selectively reduced hippocampal connectivity with occipital cortex, comprising left calcarine and lateral occipital clusters, and reduced hippocampal activity during encoding. In contrast, 8 Hz tACS reduced connectivity between the stimulation site and right early visual cortex. Neither frequency modulated hippocampal-cortical connectivity during retrieval. These results suggest that slow theta oscillations can shape hippocampal-cortical network dynamics in a frequency-specific manner, influencing the construction of temporal relations in memory.

item.title: Pyramidal Columns Acting as Attention Heads
item.description:
Relevance: 32% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition
Fabrizia Giulia Garavaglia, Marco Giunti
arXiv:2611.16057v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Can the functional architecture of a Transformer attention head be given a biological construction? More specifically, could a suitable group of pyramidal columns in posterior temporal language regions (PTLRs) constitute the biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head, under a mathematical instantiation that need not coincide with its standard Transformer instantiation? This paper investigates this hypothesis by examining possible correspondences between the functional organization of attention heads and neurophysiological mechanisms operating within and across pyramidal columns involved in human language processing. Our analysis builds on a mechanical-structural description of Transformer attention heads as systems of simple neural networks linked through output-input and output-weight interconnections. We examine the functional organization of an attention head and the input-dependent transformations it produces, and ask how the corresponding processing relations could be constructed in biological neural tissue. We then identify candidate neural mechanisms of signal transmission and modulation within and across pyramidal columns that may jointly support such a construction. On this basis, we propose that a suitably organized group of pyramidal columns in PTLRs could constitute a biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head. Whether the required functional organization actually exists in PTLRs remains an open empirical question. The hypothesis does not require the biological system to reproduce the standard mathematical instantiation of Transformer attention: the same functional architecture may be mechanically realized and mathematically instantiated in a different way, consistent with its biological construction.

item.title: Solvable dynamical model of in-context learning
item.description:
Relevance: 31% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Ruoran Bai, Haiping Huang
arXiv:2611.00921v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pretrained Transformer architectures display a surprising in-context learning ability without additional training. How the learning process guides the network to achieve this intriguing capability remains unsolved. In this study, we focus on a single-layer single-head linear attention model, where an empirical risk minimization is defined for learning. Given a finite number of training examples, we determine the exact solution of network-parameter dynamics, which is linked to the training error and generalization error, characterizing how memorization and generalization emerge from learning and how these transitions are related to curvatures of the empirical risk landscape. Furthermore, we calculate a data-dependent free energy, from which the training and generalization errors in the long time limit of learning dynamics can be well predicted. Our work adds insights toward understanding the mechanism of in-context learning especially from a learning dynamics perspective.

item.title: Geometrically Disentangling Concept Learning from the Language Modeling Loss
item.description:
Relevance: 31% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Yupei Wang, Neil Mallinar, Mikhail Belkin, Alex Warstadt
arXiv:2611.18933v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models acquire a vast array of concepts and abilities from next-token prediction alone. We introduce an interpretability framework that exposes how this single loss relates to the development of different concepts at different points during pretraining. We propose Concept Energy, a measure of the concept-specific alignment between a concept subspace and the average gradient outer product (AGOP) of the next-token-prediction loss. The concept subspace captures where the concept currently lives in the model's representation; AGOP captures the directions to which the loss is most sensitive. Across 19 checkpoints of Pythia-410M and -1B and 12 lexical, syntactic, and semantic concepts, we find that the first peak in Concept Energy generally occurs at or before the steepest increase in probe decodability. Furthermore, whereas probe performance usually increases monotonically throughout training, Concept Energy is not confined to a single peak; some concepts exhibit sustained or repeated engagement across pretraining, suggesting that concept learning may require continual reinforcement or occur at multiple points. Our results indicate that the loss contributes to concept learning in a myriad of ways that simple probe performance alone cannot reveal.

item.title: Adaptive Anisotropic Attention for Axis-Structured Signals
item.description:
Relevance: 31% | Source: arXiv AI
Mahir Jain, Parshva Runwal, Aditya Ray Mishra, Raj Singh Bani, Arvasu Kulkarni, Sandeep Singh, Siddharth Panwar
arXiv:2609.08788v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Dense self-attention treats all token pairs as equally plausible before learning, an interaction-isotropic prior that can be mismatched to structured signals. For structured, low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) signals such as EEG, dependencies are organized along the electrode and time axes, and this uniform prior exposes each token to many irrelevant interactions. We introduce Adaptive Anisotropic Attention (AAA), which splits attention into two paths: a temporal path, where each token attends to the tokens of its own electrode across time, and a spatial path, where it attends to the tokens of the other electrodes at the same time step. A small gate predicts, for every token, a convex combination of the two path outputs: two non-negative weights that sum to one. On six EEG downstream tasks, the resulting model, AXON (AXis-factorized Operator Network), improves mean balanced accuracy over a dense baseline under both linear probing and full fine-tuning. We show that both paths (temporal and spatial) are necessary and that the weighted sum beats a hard choice of one path; most of the benefit comes from the gate learning a different temporal/spatial balance at each layer of the network. Controlled audio spectrogram experiments show that axis factorization transfers beyond EEG. These results suggest that aligning attention with the natural axes of structured signals provides a useful inductive bias.

item.title: TIDE: Asymmetric Neural Circuits for Stabilized Temporal Inhibitory-Excitatory Dynamics
item.description:
Relevance: 31% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Alexander Kyuroson, Denis Kleyko, Marcus Liwicki
arXiv:2605.19403v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent Continuous Thought Machine (CTM) architecture decouples internal computation from external inputs via neural dynamics, but relies on unconstrained multi-layer perceptrons for its recurrent computations. We propose to model neural dynamics using asymmetric Excitatory-Inhibitory (E-I) networks, which can be stabilized via principles from network theory, while obeying Dale's principle and can be expressed as energy-based systems optimized through a game-theoretic loss. Building on this perspective, we introduce Temporal Inhibitory-Excitatory Dynamic Engine (TIDE), a neuro-inspired architecture that computes internal representations through neural dynamics stabilized by incorporating the Wilson-Cowan dynamics and lateral inhibition. TIDE balances biological realism by, for instance, using Hierarchical Receptive Fields and enforcing Dale's principle to ensure a realistic $80:20$ E-I balance ratio with an end-to-end trainable architecture. The aim of this paper is to introduce a new architecture that brings neuro-inspired learning and architectural principles to the forefront. We present proofs of convergence, stability, and complexity bounds, along with empirical ablation studies. Overall, TIDE achieves higher $\texttt{top-1}$ accuracy than CTM on the majority of the investigated datasets while requiring a smaller training budget. Furthermore, across varying training budgets, TIDE improves $\texttt{top-1}$ accuracy on ImageNet-C by an average of $+1.65$% to $+6.42$% under different perturbation severity levels.

item.title: Dance experience shapes local brain dynamics and shared responses during naturalistic action observation
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Chang, D., Song, D., Rao, H.
Skilled action observation unfolds over time: viewers follow changing movements, coordinate what they see with prior experience, and form a response to the performance as a whole. Dance expertise is known to alter action-related activation and the similarity of spectators' responses, but its association with local BOLD dynamics during an extended performance remains unclear. We reanalyzed fMRI from 14 professional dancers and 11 novices watching the same 33-minute dance film; one choreographer provided a separate reference. In the first 678 volumes, we measured voxelwise brain entropy (BEN) using sample entropy before summarizing it in Schaefer 400 parcels and seven networks, calculated windowed entropy from parcel-mean signals, and examined intersubject correlation (ISC) and four group-blind coactivation patterns (CAPs). After adjustment for local gray-matter volume, age, sex, and motion, dancers had higher static BEN in 32 parcels and six networks (FDR q < .05). Dynamic BEN was higher in control and default-mode networks. Dancer-dancer ISC exceeded novice-novice ISC in five networks. Dancers occupied one common CAP less often and another more often, while performer synchrony and acceleration tracked state occurrence across spectators. These converging observations show that dance experience is expressed in local temporal irregularity, shared spectator responses, and the distribution of brain states during naturalistic action observation.

item.title: NeuroMASS v4: Geometry-Aware Neural Population Dynamics via Learnable Hyperbolic Latent Representations and Biologically-Calibrated Diagonal State Space Models
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Singh, R., Cherukuri, J. V., Somanna, A.
The geometry of neural population activity is a fundamental challenge in computational neuroscience. We present NeuroMASS v4, a novel architecture that introduces learnable hyperbolic latent geometry to spike-train co-smoothing on the Neural Latents Benchmark (NLB'21). Our central scientific claim is that the curvature c of a Poincar&eacute-ball--learned end-to-end from extracellular spike recordings--constitutes a biologically interpretable geometric signature: significantly positive for ring-manifold motor circuits (MC_Maze, MC_RTT) and near-zero for topologically unstructured frontal circuits (DMFC_RSG). The architecture unifies five principled components: (i) discrete spike-count embed- dings with learned neuron-identity vectors, (ii) permutation-equivariant attention-weighted neuron pooling, (iii) a diagonal S4D state space model initialised with a log-uniform frequency prior spanning 2-200 Hz, (iv) a Poincar&eacute-ball projection with learnable scalar curvature, and (v) a Frobenius-bounded session adapter. Training uses masked self-prediction of spike counts with an auxiliary behaviour decoding objective; all experiments use exclusively real DANDI/NLB recordings under a strict fail-stop data policy. We report results across four NLB datasets spanning motor, somatosensory, and cognitive cortices in rhesus macaque, and demonstrate that learned curvature statistically predicts circuit topology.

item.title: Neurocognitive signatures of intrinsic motivation in naturalistic information seeking and memory
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Su, H., Knight, C., Liu, P. R., Lee, H.
Humans often seek information without direct external reward. Theories distinguish two major dimensions of this intrinsic motivation: wanting, the desire to resolve an information gap, and liking, the enjoyment of the information itself. However, how these motivational dimensions shape self-guided information-seeking behavior, neural activity, and memory formation in realworld contexts remains underexplored. To address this gap, we developed a naturalistic fMRI paradigm in which participants freely browsed the internet, subsequently recalled their browsing experiences, and retrospectively reported their moment-to-moment wanting and liking. We found that both dimensions predicted more stable browsing trajectories but engaged partially dissociable neural systems: wanting recruited regions supporting goal-directed cognition, whereas liking engaged affective regions. Wanting and liking also interacted to predict memory, with wanting predicting recall primarily when liking was low. Compared with active browsing, passive viewing of the same web content reduced wanting and liking and diminished their dissociation, yet both continued to predict memory and intersubject neural similarity in the default mode network. These findings show that naturally fluctuating wanting and liking guide how we seek and remember information through overlapping yet distinct neurocognitive mechanisms.

item.title: NI-ACT: A Neural Intent Interface for Brain-Embodied Manipulation
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv AI
Yinghao Li, WeiHsien Lee, Zeyu Zhang, Canyang Zhao, Ke Fang, Xing Li, Bing Liu
arXiv:2611.19332v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Intracortical brain-computer interfaces can drive robotic arms, but they keep the user inside the fast sensorimotor loop: every approach, correction, and grasp must be neurally specified. Whether intracortical population activity can instead serve as a task-level condition for a learned embodied policy, without symbolic commands or hand-designed skill libraries, remains unknown. NI-ACT addresses this question with a hierarchical brain-embodied framework: a brief motor-cortical signal is read once as a persistent intent, and a visuomotor policy then closes the perception-action loop from vision and proprioception. In a counterfactual grasping task where the scene cannot specify the target, the neural intent alone determined which object the robot grasped; replacing the intent changed the behavior accordingly. Passing the full population latent as a dedicated intent token, rather than a one-hot decoded direction, raised grasp completion from 69% to 81% over 132 held-out scenes, whereas a continuous direction alone did not improve on a one-hot label. Where the signal was read also mattered: in one dual-array session, with the readout window matched, premotor (PMd) intent completed more grasps than primary motor (M1) intent (77% vs. 53%), and the conventional post-cue M1 readout reached 42%. Preparatory activity was itself sufficient: in a center-out task, intent read only from PMd before the go cue (that is, before any movement) drove complete grasps, and in one recording it completed more grasps than the same animal's post-cue readout. These results show that how a neural signal is represented, and where and when it is read, jointly determine how effectively it conveys movement goals to an embodied agent.

item.title: Temporal Regularized Learning: Self-Supervised Learning Local in Space and Time
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Davide Wiest
arXiv:2611.17019v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Self-supervised objectives such as VICReg learn representations by making related inputs similar, while variance and covariance penalties prevent collapse. These penalties are statistics over a batch of samples, so layer-local variants, too, are typically local in space but not in time. We introduce Temporal Regularized Learning (TeReL), which optimizes a VICReg-style objective one sample at a time with purely local updates: each update uses only the current activity of its own and the preceding layer and a fixed-size running state. Temporally adjacent inputs serve as positive pairs, which makes the objective a soft form of Slow Feature Analysis (SFA). Running estimates of each neuron's mean and variance, together with one lateral matrix per layer, replace the batch statistics; held fixed during differentiation, they turn the gradient into a Hebbian feedforward update and an anti-Hebbian lateral update. We show that a two-layer network trained with batch size one on an MNIST stream of class-homogeneous chunks reaches 96.48% linear-probe accuracy, above random features (95.09%) and classical SFA, and that the temporal order and each loss term contribute to this result. With both locality constraints relaxed, the same objective matches supervised backpropagation. TeReL thus shows that the collapse-preventing statistics of modern self-supervised learning can be held as running state at each neuron, which brings these objectives closer to what brains and neuromorphic hardware can implement.

item.title: Connectivity from activity in spiking neural networks
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition
Albert J. Wakhloo, Sebastian Mizera
arXiv:2611.21592v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We show that a wide range of recurrent neural network models obey a simple set of equations tying synaptic connectivity and single-cell response properties to neural correlations. Our modeling framework considers networks in a stationary, asynchronous state and contains a broad class of synaptic filters, spiking nonlinearities, and random-plus-structured connectivity. The resulting equations naturally decompose into contributions from monosynaptic, disynaptic, and higher order paths through the network. We leverage this decomposition to express the effective monosynaptic connection between two neurons in terms of experimentally measurable statistics of the activity, and in particular, their high-frequency correlations. In this way, we show that it is possible to recover network connectivity from neural activity.

item.title: Anchoring Motion, Refining Trajectories: Generalizable Continuous Neural Decoding
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition
Fanqi Shen, Junru Chen, Surui Cheng, Jiahe Li, ZhiZhang Yuan, Gaorui Zhang, ZhiYuan Cao, Xiaoquan Shen, Yang Yang
arXiv:2611.21335v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Brain activity encodes motor information across multiple temporal scales, enabling continuous neural control beyond discrete action recognition. However, existing methods are typically tailored to specific subjects and tasks, with direct neural-to-kinematic mappings that can entangle subject-specific neural variability with task-dependent motion patterns, limiting generalization. To address these limitations, we introduce AMRT, a shared neural decoding framework for heterogeneous electrode configurations and movement paradigms. Motivated by cortical encoding of movement direction and speed, AMRT adopts a two-stage design that anchors local motion through velocity estimation and refines the resulting trajectories over longer horizons, encouraging reuse of local motion tendencies across subjects and tasks. Across three datasets, AMRT generalizes to unseen trials and subjects and demonstrates transfer potential across neural recordings and movement paradigms, highlighting the potential of shared neural representations and anchor-and-refine decoding for generalizable continuous neural control.

item.title: Analyzing Memory Effects in Large Language Models through the lens of Cognitive Psychology
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition
Zhaoyang Cao, Lael Schooler, Reza Zafarani
arXiv:2509.17138v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Memory, a fundamental component of human cognition, exhibits adaptive yet fallible characteristics as illustrated by Schacter's memory "sins".These cognitive phenomena have been studied extensively in psychology and neuroscience, but the extent to which artificial systems, specifically Large Language Models (LLMs), emulate these cognitive phenomena remains underexplored. This study uses human memory research as a lens for understanding LLMs and systematically investigates human memory effects in state-of-the-art LLMs using paradigms drawn from psychological research. We evaluate seven key memory phenomena, comparing human behavior to LLM performance. Both people and models remember less when overloaded with information (list length effect) and remember better with repeated exposure (list strength effect). They also show similar difficulties when retrieving overlapping information, where storing too many similar facts leads to confusion (fan effect). Like humans, LLMs are susceptible to falsely "remembering" words that were never shown but are related to others (false memories), and they can apply prior learning to new, related situations (cross-domain generalization). However, LLMs differ in two key ways: they are less influenced by the order in which information is presented (positional bias) and more robust when processing random or meaningless material (nonsense effect). These results reveal both alignments and divergences in how LLMs and humans reconstruct memory. The findings help clarify how memory-like behavior in LLMs echoes core features of human cognition, while also highlighting the architectural differences that lead to distinct patterns of error and success.

item.title: Func-JEPA: Learning a Sobolev Space of Functions as Latent Vectors
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv AI
Alejandro Moreno Arcas
arXiv:2611.19542v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Pretraining an encoder once and reusing it across tasks is a widespread approach in vision and language. However, neural symbolic mathematics still trains a dedicated sequence-to-sequence model for each task, so that no representation of a function is shared. In this work, we propose the Function Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (Func-JEPA, abbreviated f-JEPA): an encoder of mathematical functions, pretrained on their symbolic form, whose latent space imitates the Sobolev space H^1 and in which differentiation is a learned latent operator. The norm of a latent is computed exactly from the function, whereas its direction is learned to match Sobolev angles. The frozen encoder is then reused by lightweight modules for decoding, composition, integration, and regression from samples. The representation and four downstream tasks are evaluated within and outside the pretraining distribution. f-JEPA recovers exact formulas from noisy samples more often than the compared symbolic-regression methods, whereas computer algebra and task-specific models remain stronger on standard integration and differential-equation benchmarks.

item.title: Correlated but distinct: VIP and NDNF interneurons implement dissociable inhibitory motifs for state-dependent gain control in visual cortex
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Jenks, K. R., Ahrlund-Richter, S., Celotto, M., Sipe, G., Sur, M.
VIP and NDNF positive interneurons are both found in layers 1 and 2/3 of the cortex, but have distinct patterns of gene expression, morphology, and connectivity. Despite this, their functional roles in the sensory cortices seem remarkably similar; their activity correlates with behavioral state, and they gate behaviorally driven increases in excitatory activity and sensory-driven responses. We sought to directly compare VIP and NDNF positive interneurons in the mouse visual cortex to determine if their activity was indeed functionally redundant or could be distinguished by their correlation to behavioral state, to excitatory activity, or to excitatory visual responses. Using simultaneous recordings of pupil diameter and running speed together with dual-population calcium imaging, we found that although the activity of both VIP and NDNF positive interneurons was more strongly correlated with behavior than was excitatory neuron activity, VIP positive interneuron activity was more strongly correlated with pupil diameter, whereas layer 2/3 NDNF positive interneuron activity was more strongly correlated with running speed. Excitatory-to-VIP pairwise correlation increased during locomotion, whereas excitatory-to-NDNF pairwise correlation decreased during locomotion. Intriguingly, although VIP-to-NDNF pairwise correlation was high, cortical depth significantly affected both VIP-to-NDNF correlation and the correlation of NDNF positive interneurons with pupil diameter and running speed. As expected, excitatory visual responses were significantly modulated by both pupil dilation and locomotion. However, we found that the level of VIP and NDNF activity preceding stimulus onset had a unique contribution to and was positively correlated with the amplitude of excitatory visual responses. Thus, while highly correlated to one another and to behavioral state, VIP and NDNF positive interneurons are functionally distinguishable in their relationship to both behavior and excitatory activity in the mouse visual cortex.

item.title: Analysis choices can produce apparent rich-club differences: an Alzheimer's disease EEG case study
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition
Kai-Wayne Liu, Ryan Tian En Pang, Pholpat Durongbhan
arXiv:2611.19708v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The weighted rich-club coefficient tests whether a network's most strongly connected nodes are preferentially interconnected. Its interpretation depends on two often-implicit choices that are easy to overlook: how the randomised comparison networks are constructed, and whether the hubs are re-identified in each comparison network or held fixed at those of the observed network. When hubs are defined by connection strength, these choices change what the coefficient actually tests. We examined how these choices affect inference using resting-state EEG from 20 people with Alzheimer's disease and 20 controls. Holding the data fixed, we compared four analysis pipelines, crossing two ways of building the comparison networks with the two hub choices, and ran a calibration study in which the same pipelines were applied to data constructed to contain no preferential hub coupling. An apparent eyes-open group difference in rich-club organisation appeared under only one of the four pipelines, the one combining a global weight reshuffle with re-identified hubs, and was absent under the other three. More tellingly, that same pipeline reported a group difference in 40% of cases where none was present, almost always higher in the Alzheimer's disease group, while the other three stayed near the expected 5%. This shows that the same data can support or dissolve an apparent rich-club difference depending on choices that are rarely reported. No single choice is universally correct, but reporting which were made, and why they fit the question being asked, is essential to interpreting the result.

item.title: What Does Hard-Negative Fine-Tuning Teach Multimodal Large Language Models? Controlled Evidence from a Compositional Benchmark
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Ranjith Chodavarapu
arXiv:2611.18701v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Fine-tuning on hard negatives is a popular way to improve the compositional reasoning of vision-language models, but when accuracy goes up it is rarely clear what the model actually learned. We ask this question for multimodal large language models. We use CompHall, 2,860 forced-choice questions (spatial, attribute, counting and part-whole) with two graded hard negatives each, three model families (LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT and Idefics2), and controls that such studies often lack: gray-image evaluation, three seeds, option-order tests, control arms trained on different question types, and independent benchmarks. We find four things. First, CompHall is not a pure test of vision: part-whole questions can be answered from the text alone (66-95% without the image), and per-image accuracy is unrelated to an object-hallucination probe (r = -0.05), so we see no evidence that compositional failures drive hallucination. Second, the original fine-tuning method scored mostly image-placeholder tokens and hurt both LLaVA models. With a corrected loss, fine-tuning raises accuracy on the spatial-relation questions of CV-Bench in all three families, by +3.2, +23.1 and +6.0 points (averaged over both option orders). Control arms show that the gain needs spatial training questions, and for LLaVA-NeXT about two-thirds of it appears even on relation words that were only wrong options in training. Third, the gain is not general: on CompHall itself it is significant only for LLaVA-NeXT (+6.9 points) and not detectable for Idefics2, it reaches about 3 points at most on true/false statements, and LLaVA-1.5 fine-tuned on other question types learns to answer "true" too often. Fourth, both losses raise the yes-bias of LLaVA-1.5 on POPE.

item.title: Why Steering Works: Toward a Unified View of Language Model Parameter Dynamics
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Ziwen Xu, Chenyan Wu, Hengyu Sun, Haiwen Hong, Mengru Wang, Yunzhi Yao, Longtao Huang, Hui Xue, Shumin Deng, Zhixuan Chu, Huajun Chen, Ningyu Zhang
arXiv:2602.02343v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Methods for controlling large language models (LLMs), including local weight fine-tuning, LoRA-based adaptation, and activation-based interventions, are often studied in isolation, obscuring their connections and making comparison difficult. In this work, we present a unified view that frames these interventions as dynamic weight updates induced by a control signal, placing them within a single conceptual framework. Building on this view, we propose a unified preference-utility analysis that separates control effects into preference, defined as the tendency toward a target concept, and utility, defined as coherent and task-valid generation, and measures both on a shared log-odds scale using polarity-paired contrastive examples. Across methods, we observe a consistent trade-off between preference and utility: stronger control increases preference while predictably reducing utility. We further explain this behavior through an activation manifold perspective, in which control shifts representations along target-concept directions to enhance preference, while utility declines primarily when interventions push representations off the model's valid-generation manifold. Finally, we introduce a new steering approach SPLIT guided by this analysis that improves preference while better preserving utility. Code is available at https://github.com/zjunlp/EasyEdit/blob/main/examples/SPLIT.md.

item.title: The Geometry of Conceptors in Neural-Activation Spaces
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Ilias Triantafyllopoulos, Young Min Cho, Ren Tao, Miranda Muqing Miao, Sunny Rai, Lyle Ungar, Sharath Chandra Guntuku, Sunghye Cho, Tyler Moore, Neville Ryant, Jo\~ao Sedoc
arXiv:2611.19075v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conceptors represent concepts as graded collections of directions in neural-activation space rather than as single vectors. We develop a geometric account of how these representations depend on the contrast used to define a concept: opposing values in bipolar fitting, or presence and absence in unipolar fitting. We derive an exact decomposition of a centered pooled conceptor into an average pole filter, a mean-separation update, and a covariance-shape update. Experiments across five language models on sentiment, political leaning and stance, and depression expression show that both updates improve reconstruction of held-out contrasts. Additional directions preserve variation beyond the mean-difference line, and changing the comparator changes the benefit of these directions. Shape, size, and overlap each show up downstream: in amplification experiments, bipolar fits raise evidence for both poles more consistently than unipolar fits; conceptor size (the quota) correlates positively with layerwise probe performance; and cross-concept overlap quantifies interference under subspace removal, linking shared directions to Boolean composition. In an additional generation evaluation, conceptor filters achieve higher target-expression win rates against an unsteered reference than three mean-based controls. Together, these findings explain how fitting choices shape conceptor geometry and support bipolar fitting when the objective is to amplify both opposing poles.

item.title: Seeing but Not Thinking: Routing Distraction in Multimodal Mixture-of-Experts
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Haolei Xu, Haiwen Hong, Hongxing Li, Rui Zhou, Yang Zhang, Longtao Huang, Hui Xue, Yongliang Shen, Weiming Lu, Yueting Zhuang
arXiv:2604.08541v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multimodal Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have achieved remarkable performance on vision-language tasks. However, we identify a puzzling phenomenon termed Seeing but Not Thinking: models accurately perceive image content yet fail in subsequent reasoning, while correctly solving identical problems presented as pure text. Through systematic analysis, we first verify that cross-modal semantic sharing exists in MoE architectures, ruling out semantic alignment failure as the sole explanation. We then reveal that visual experts and domain experts exhibit layer-wise separation, with image inputs inducing significant routing divergence from text inputs in middle layers where domain experts concentrate. Based on these findings, we propose the Routing Distraction hypothesis: when processing visual inputs, the routing mechanism fails to adequately activate task-relevant reasoning experts. To validate this hypothesis, we design a routing-guided intervention method that enhances domain expert activation. Experiments on three multimodal MoE models across six benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements, with gains of up to 3.17% on complex visual reasoning tasks. Our analysis further reveals that domain expert identification locates cognitive functions rather than sample-specific solutions, enabling effective transfer across tasks with different information structures.

item.title: How Large Are Hemispheric Asymmetries Really? — A Neurosynth Meta-Analysis
item.description:
Relevance: 25% | Source: SocArXiv
Sina Lorenz
Hemispheric asymmetries are considered a fundamental organisational principle of the human brain (Güntürkün et al., 2020). It remains unclear how pronounced these asymmetries are across different cognitive systems. This master's thesis quantifies the hemispheric asymmetries of five cognitive systems: language processing, visuospatial processing, face processing, emotional processing and motor processing. Laterality indices are computed from Neurosynth meta-analytic maps (Yarkoni et al., 2011). Based on previous findings, left-hemispheric dominance is expected for language, positive emotions and motor control. Right-hemispheric dominance is expected for visuospatial attention and face processing (e.g., Ocklenburg & Güntürkün, 2024).

item.title: Effects of sensorimotor and coordinative demands in cognitive-motor dual-task trainings for improvement of cognitive performance
item.description:
Relevance: 25% | Source: SocArXiv
Stefan Debener et al.
This study examines whether motor complexity modulates cognitive outcomes following an acute cognitive–motor dual-task (CM-DT) intervention. While previous research suggests that combined cognitive and motor demands can enhance cognition (e.g., Wollesen et al., 2020), the role of coordinative demands in acute settings is less clear. In this study, we aim to systematically manipulate sensorimotor demands in an acute CM-DT intervention as compared to the respective single-task conditions. The primary aim of the present study is to investigate whether increasing motor complexity during an acute CM-DT intervention leads to greater improvements in attention, inhibitory control and processing speed from pre- to post-test. As a secondary objective, the study examines the performance during the intervention itself by assessing dual-task effects at the behavioral and motor level.

item.title: Thinking With AI, Reasoning Without It: Cognitive Offloading to Generative AI Weakens Effort Regulation
item.description:
Relevance: 24% | Source: SocArXiv
Dawid Ratajczyk et al.
Generative artificial intelligence (genAI) is increasingly used to support learning and problem solving, but it remains unclear how relying on such support affects people's ability to reason independently afterwards. We investigated whether using genAI to solve a complex reasoning task influences subsequent reasoning, memory, and effort when the technology is no longer available. In a preregistered laboratory experiment with a final sample of 193 participants, we used a three-stage relational reasoning task developed for the study, in which participants learned and reasoned about a network of fictional entities and their relationships. During the first stage, participants completed the task either with or without access to ChatGPT, while performance incentives were independently manipulated. All participants then completed a more complex reasoning task based on the same relational network without genAI support, followed by a memory test. GenAI support improved accuracy during the initial task and reduced perceived difficulty. In the subsequent unaided reasoning task, prior genAI use was associated with some evidence of poorer independent reasoning. GenAI use was also associated with weaker adjustment of effort to incentives and task difficulty once the tool was removed. No clear effects were observed on later memory. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of distinguishing successful AI-assisted task completion from the knowledge construction and effort regulation needed to apply the same information independently.
